heading: What is Temporal & Why It Exists
subheading: A durable workflow orchestration platform that makes distributed applications reliable
description:
Temporal is a workflow orchestration platform designed to make distributed, long-running applications reliable. Created to solve the hardest problems in distributed systems — failures, retries, state management, timers, coordination, and recovery.

The core idea is Durable Execution — a workflow can continue making progress even if the process or machine executing it crashes. Temporal persists the workflow's history and state, and can replay the workflow on another Worker to resume exactly where it left off.

Why do we need Temporal?
Modern distributed systems involve multiple services, queues, databases, and external APIs. Failures can happen at any point. Without an orchestration engine, your application code has to manually manage retries, state persistence, recovery, timers, idempotency, coordination, compensation, and failure handling. This leads to fragile, complex code that is hard to test and maintain.

Temporal moves all of this responsibility into the platform. You write your business logic as straightforward code, and Temporal handles the infrastructure concerns.

The strongest mental model:
"Temporal Server remembers and coordinates; Workers execute."

In a 30-second explanation: Temporal lets you define a Workflow as the business process and Activities for external operations. The Temporal Server durably stores workflow history and coordinates tasks, timers, retries, and recovery. Workers execute your actual Workflow and Activity code. If a Worker crashes, Temporal replays the persisted history on another Worker and continues execution. Signals allow external systems to send information asynchronously to an already-running Workflow.

heading: Core Concepts
subheading: The fundamental building blocks — Workflows, Activities, Workers, Task Queues, and Executions
description:
**Workflow:**
Defines the durable business process or orchestration. This is your core business logic — the sequence of steps that need to happen. Workflow code must be deterministic because Temporal replays it for recovery.

**Activity:**
Performs external, non-deterministic work — database operations, HTTP calls, file I/O, calls to external services. Activities are where side effects happen. They can fail and be retried independently.

**Worker:**
A long-running process in your infrastructure that executes your Workflow and Activity implementations. Workers poll Temporal Server for tasks and report results back.

**Temporal Server:**
The durable coordinator that stores workflow history and state, manages task queues, timers, and coordinates execution. It does NOT execute your application code.

**Task Queue:**
A logical queue used to route Workflow Tasks and Activity Tasks to Workers. Workers register on specific task queues and poll them for work.

**Workflow Execution:**
One durable, running instance of a Workflow. Each execution is identified by a Workflow ID (business-level) and a Run ID (unique per run).

**Event History:**
A durable, ordered record of every important event in a Workflow Execution — activity scheduled, activity completed, signal received, timer fired, etc. This is the foundation of recovery and deterministic replay.

**Workflow Task:**
A task sent to a Worker saying: "Process this Workflow's history and decide what should happen next."

**Activity Task:**
A task sent to a Worker saying: "Execute this specific external operation."

heading: Temporal Server Architecture
subheading: The internal components that coordinate workflow execution
description:
The Temporal Server consists of several internal services working together:

• **Frontend Service** — receives all client and Worker API requests (RPC calls). This is the entry point for starting workflows, sending signals, and polling for tasks.

• **History Service** — maintains workflow execution state and history. It coordinates workflow progression, persists events, and manages the lifecycle of each Workflow Execution.

• **Matching Service** — manages task queues. It matches available tasks (Workflow Tasks and Activity Tasks) with Workers that are polling those queues.

• **Worker Service** — handles internal Temporal server-side background processing (archival, replication, etc.). Important: this is NOT the same as your application's Temporal Worker.

• **Persistence Layer** — the durable storage (typically Cassandra, MySQL, or PostgreSQL) used by Temporal for workflow state, history, and server metadata.

Deployment models:
• **Temporal Cloud** — Temporal Inc. operates the server infrastructure. Your Workers connect to Temporal Cloud over the network. You only manage your Workers.
• **Self-Hosted** — your company deploys and operates Temporal Server on Kubernetes, VMs, Docker, etc. You manage both the server infrastructure and your Workers.

The exact deployment topology varies, but the architecture is the same regardless of hosting model.

heading: Server vs Worker — Who Does What
subheading: The most important distinction — Temporal Server coordinates, Workers execute your code
description:
This is the most critical concept to understand:

Temporal Server does NOT execute your Workflow or Activity code.

Your Workflow and Activity code runs inside your Worker process, in your infrastructure. The Temporal Server only coordinates — it stores history, manages task queues, handles timers, and tells Workers what to do next.

Your Java application structure:
  Your Java Service
    └── Temporal Java SDK
        └── Worker
            ├── Workflow implementation
            └── Activity implementation

Where Workers run:
Workers run in YOUR infrastructure — inside your Kubernetes pods, Docker containers, VMs, or application processes. Each service that uses Temporal has its own Worker.

How Workers get work:
Workers do not receive HTTP requests from your application for each task. Instead, Workers poll the Temporal Server for work through Temporal's SDK and task queue mechanisms:
  1. Worker polls Temporal Server for a task on its registered task queue.
  2. Temporal returns a task (if available).
  3. Worker executes the Workflow or Activity code.
  4. Worker reports the result back to Temporal.

This polling model means Workers pull work — they are not pushed to.

heading: Workflow Execution Flow
subheading: Step-by-step — what happens from starting a workflow to completion
description:
When you call WorkflowClient.start(workflow::processTransaction, transaction), here is what happens:

1. Client Stub — the Workflow Stub acts as a proxy and sends a StartWorkflowExecution RPC to Temporal Server.
2. Validation — Temporal validates the Workflow ID, reuse policy, task queue, workflow type, input, and retry configuration.
3. Create Execution — Temporal creates the Workflow Execution, assigns a Workflow ID and Run ID.
4. Persist History — Temporal durably records the initial workflow events and schedules the first Workflow Task.
5. Task Queue — the Workflow Task is placed on the appropriate task queue.
6. Worker Polls — a Worker polling that queue receives the Workflow Task.
7. Replay & Execute — the Temporal SDK inside the Worker replays the workflow history and executes the workflow code deterministically.
8. Produce Commands — the workflow code may produce commands: Schedule Activity, Start Timer, Start Child Workflow, Complete Workflow, Fail Workflow, etc.
9. Report Back — the Worker reports the Workflow Task completion and its commands back to Temporal.
10. Record & Schedule — Temporal records the resulting events and schedules whatever work is required next (Activity Tasks, timer events, etc.).

This cycle repeats — Workflow Task → Worker → Commands → Temporal → next task — until the Workflow reaches a terminal state (Completed, Failed, Cancelled, Terminated).

**execute() vs start():**
• execute() — starts the Workflow and waits synchronously for its result. Blocks until the Workflow completes.
• start() — starts the Workflow asynchronously and returns a WorkflowExecution object immediately. The Workflow continues independently under Temporal's coordination.

heading: Durable Execution & Deterministic Replay
subheading: How Temporal recovers workflows after crashes — and why your code must be deterministic
description:
**Durable Execution:**
Temporal can recover workflow progress despite infrastructure or process failures. If a Worker crashes mid-execution, another Worker picks up the Workflow Task, replays the stored history, reconstructs the workflow state, and continues from where it left off. No work is lost because the history is durably stored by Temporal Server.

Example:
  Worker A executes workflow → crashes → Worker B replays history → continues workflow.

**Deterministic Replay:**
Temporal does NOT serialize your Java objects and move them to another machine. Instead, the SDK reconstructs workflow state by replaying the event history through your workflow code. Each event in the history tells the SDK what happened — which activities were scheduled, what results came back, which timers fired, etc.

Because the SDK replays your workflow code against the history, the code must be deterministic — it must make the same decisions every time it runs with the same history.

**What you must NOT do in Workflow code:**
• Direct random number generation (use Workflow.newRandom()).
• Direct system time access for decisions (use Workflow.currentTimeMillis()).
• Direct network calls or database calls (use Activities instead).
• Arbitrary thread management.
• Any operation whose result could differ between executions.

**What is safe in Workflow code:**
• Workflow timers (Workflow.sleep(), Workflow.await()).
• Workflow time APIs.
• Workflow random APIs.
• Activities for all external side effects.

Workflow Tasks provide checkpoint boundaries — after each Workflow Task, Temporal durably records the resulting events, enabling future replay.

heading: Signals
subheading: Sending asynchronous messages to an already-running Workflow
description:
A Signal is an asynchronous message sent to an existing Workflow Execution. It provides new information to a running workflow without starting a new one.

**Mental model:**
• Start Workflow = create a new durable process.
• Signal Workflow = send information to an existing durable process.

**How signaling works internally:**
1. Your application calls workflow.approvePayment() — this sends a SignalWorkflowExecution RPC to Temporal Server.
2. Temporal finds the Workflow Execution by its Workflow ID.
3. Temporal durably records the signal in the workflow history.
4. A Workflow Task is scheduled and placed on the task queue.
5. A Worker picks up the task, replays the workflow history, and the SDK invokes the registered @SignalMethod handler.
6. The handler modifies workflow state (e.g., approved = true).
7. If the workflow was waiting with Workflow.await(() -> approved), the condition is now satisfied and the workflow continues.

Signals are NOT direct method calls from your application to the Worker. The signal always goes through Temporal Server, is durably persisted, and is delivered through the task/replay mechanism.

**Why signals are durable:**
If a Worker crashes after Temporal records the signal but before processing it, the signal is not lost. Another Worker replays the history (including the signal event) and processes it.

Signals can carry data — for example: @SignalMethod void updateAmount(BigDecimal amount). A workflow can receive multiple different signals (approve, updateAmount, cancel), each handled by its own @SignalMethod.

**Signal vs Activity:**
• Activity = "Workflow, please perform this external operation."
• Signal = "External world to Workflow — here is new information."

**Signal vs Start:**
• Start = creates a new Workflow Execution.
• Signal = communicates with an already-existing Workflow Execution.

heading: Activities, Retries & Compensation
subheading: Handling external operations, transient failures, and business-level rollbacks
description:
Activities are where all external, non-deterministic work happens — database operations, HTTP calls, API integrations, file I/O. They run inside Workers but outside the deterministic replay boundary.

Activities can fail because of:
• External service unavailability.
• Network errors.
• Database errors.
• Process crashes.
• Timeouts.

**Retry Policy:**
Temporal can automatically retry failed Activities according to a configurable Retry Policy that specifies:
• Maximum number of attempts.
• Initial retry interval.
• Backoff coefficient (commonly exponential backoff).
• Maximum retry interval.
• Non-retryable error types.

**Infrastructure vs Business Failures:**
• Infrastructure failures (service temporarily unavailable, network timeout) — retries often solve the problem. Let Temporal's retry policy handle these automatically.
• Business failures (account does not exist, insufficient funds) — retrying will not help. Your application logic must decide what to do.

**Saga / Compensation Pattern:**
When a multi-step process partially succeeds and then encounters a permanent failure, you need compensation — undoing the completed steps.

Example:
  Step 1: Debit account A → succeeds.
  Step 2: Credit account B → permanently fails.
  Compensation: Reverse the debit on account A.

In Temporal, you implement this directly in your Workflow code — maintain a list of completed steps and their compensating activities, and execute compensations in reverse order when a step fails permanently. This is the Saga pattern.

heading: Workflow ID, Run ID & Idempotency
subheading: Business-level identity and uniqueness guarantees for workflow executions
description:
**Workflow ID:**
A business-level identifier that you assign when starting a Workflow. For example: "transaction-12345" or "order-payment-98765". Temporal uses the Workflow ID to identify the logical Workflow Execution.

Key rule: no two Workflow Executions with the same Workflow ID can be open simultaneously. This gives you built-in idempotency — if you try to start a workflow with an ID that is already running, Temporal rejects the duplicate.

Workflow ID Reuse Policy — controls what happens after a Workflow with that ID closes:
• Allow Reuse — a new Workflow with the same ID can be started after the previous one completes.
• Allow Reuse on Failure — reuse only if the previous run failed.
• Reject Duplicate — never allow reuse of the same Workflow ID.

This is extremely useful for enforcing business-level uniqueness. For example, using the transaction ID as the Workflow ID ensures that the same transaction is never processed twice.

**Run ID:**
A unique, system-generated identifier for a particular run of a Workflow Execution. While the Workflow ID represents the business process, the Run ID identifies one specific execution of it.

Example:
  Workflow ID = transaction-12345 (the business transaction).
  Run ID = abc-123-def-456 (this particular execution attempt).

If a Workflow is retried or restarted with the same Workflow ID, it gets a new Run ID.

heading: Long-Running Workflows & Timers
subheading: Workflows that last days, weeks, or months — without blocking threads
description:
Temporal Workflows can remain alive for minutes, hours, days, weeks, or even months. This is fundamentally different from a typical API request that completes in milliseconds.

**Durable Timers:**
A Workflow can wait using Temporal's built-in timers (Workflow.sleep(Duration.ofDays(3))). The Worker process does NOT need to remain blocked in a Java thread for three days. Instead:
1. The Workflow tells Temporal to start a timer.
2. The Worker finishes the current Workflow Task and is free to handle other work.
3. After 3 days, Temporal fires the timer event.
4. A new Workflow Task is created and sent to a Worker.
5. The Worker replays the history, sees the timer has fired, and continues the workflow.

This means long-running workflows do not consume Worker resources while waiting. The timer is managed by Temporal Server, not by your application threads.

**Common use cases:**
• Subscription billing — workflow runs for the lifetime of a subscription, waking up monthly to process payments.
• Approval processes — workflow waits indefinitely for a human to approve or reject.
• Multi-day data pipelines — workflow coordinates steps that run over several days.
• Order fulfillment — workflow tracks an order from placement through shipping and delivery.

**Testing long timers:**
Temporal provides time-skipping test facilities so you can test workflows with multi-day timers in seconds rather than waiting for the actual duration.

heading: Workflow Code Versioning
subheading: Safely evolving Workflow logic while long-running executions are still in flight
description:
**The Problem:**
A Workflow starts under V1 and may still be running days or weeks later. A new Worker deployment contains V2. If V2 changes the sequence of commands expected during replay, old histories may no longer be compatible — causing non-determinism errors.

**Example:**
V1: activityA() → activityB()
V2: activityA() → activityC() → activityB()
An old history does not contain activityC, so replaying V2 against it produces incompatible commands.

**Workflow.getVersion (Java):**
int version = Workflow.getVersion("add-activity-c", Workflow.DEFAULT_VERSION, 1);
activityA();
if (version >= 1) { activityC(); }
activityB();

Temporal records the version decision in workflow history. On replay, the workflow uses the recorded version. New executions take the new path; old histories retain the old path.

**Important rules:**
• Temporal provides versioning APIs but does NOT automatically make arbitrary code changes backward-compatible. Developers must identify and guard incompatible changes.
• Keep old code paths while relevant executions may still need them.
• Test replay against representative histories before rollout.
• Do not blindly deploy incompatible workflow code to all Workers.

**Workflow Versioning vs Worker Versioning:**
• **Workflow code versioning** (Workflow.getVersion / GetVersion) — makes changes to workflow orchestration compatible with existing histories. Records a version decision in history. Addresses determinism and command-sequence compatibility.
• **Worker Versioning / Worker Deployments** — a deployment/routing mechanism for controlling which Worker code version executes work. Can help roll out code and keep executions on compatible Worker versions. It is separate from Workflow.getVersion.
• Do not treat Worker Versioning as an automatic replacement for workflow code compatibility.

**Activity Code Changes:**
Temporal does not have a general Activity-version API analogous to Workflow.getVersion.
• If an Activity has completed — its result is in history. Replay does not re-execute it.
• If an Activity has not executed yet — it runs the implementation available on the Worker that receives the Activity Task. An old Workflow may run new Activity logic.
• If Activity behavior must be controlled — keep distinct activity types (ActivityB_V1 and ActivityB_V2) and have workflow logic choose, or use Worker Versioning for deployment-level routing.
• Make Activities idempotent and carefully manage compatibility for retries.

heading: Sticky Scheduling
subheading: A performance optimization that reduces replay overhead — not a correctness guarantee
description:
**Sticky scheduling** is a performance optimization where Temporal prefers sending subsequent Workflow Tasks to the same Worker that previously handled the Workflow, so that the Worker can reuse cached workflow state and reduce replay work.

**If the Worker crashes, restarts, loses its cache, or is unavailable:**
• Sticky scheduling is not a guarantee that the Workflow stays on that Worker.
• Another Worker can receive the Workflow Task.
• That Worker reconstructs workflow state by replaying persisted history.

**Key takeaways:**
• Sticky scheduling is not required for correctness.
• Temporal's persisted history is the source of truth.
• Sticky execution reduces replay overhead; it does not permanently assign a Workflow to one Worker.

heading: Task Queues, Pollers & Concurrency
subheading: How work is routed to Workers and how to control execution capacity
description:
**Task Queue:**
A task queue is a logical routing mechanism for delivering Workflow Tasks or Activity Tasks to compatible Workers.
• Workers poll task queues for tasks.
• Multiple Worker instances can poll the same task queue.
• Separate queues can isolate workloads and enable independent scaling/configuration.
• A task queue is not the same thing as a Worker or a physical queue server.
• A task queue belongs to a Namespace.

**Worker Replica:**
An instance/process/pod running a Temporal Worker. Adding replicas is horizontal scaling.

**Poller:**
A Worker-side component that requests tasks from Temporal Server. Pollers fetch work — they are not the same as task execution slots.

**Concurrency:**
Controls how many tasks a Worker can execute simultaneously.
• Workflow Task and Activity Task execution have separate concurrency controls.
• More pollers do not automatically mean more execution capacity.
• More replicas increase capacity only if Workers are the bottleneck and downstream systems can handle the added load.

**Go SDK example:**
worker.Options{ MaxConcurrentActivityExecutionSize: 100 }
This is an example setting, not a universal recommended value. Choose limits based on task duration, CPU/memory, polling behavior, and downstream capacity.

heading: Namespaces
subheading: Logical isolation and administration boundaries in Temporal
description:
A **Namespace** is a logical isolation and administration boundary in Temporal.

• Task queues exist within a Namespace.
• Workers must connect to the appropriate Namespace and poll the intended task queue.
• Namespaces may separate environments or workloads, such as payments-prod and payments-staging.
• Namespace separation can help operations and isolation, but does not automatically guarantee separate physical infrastructure or unlimited capacity.
• Creating more Namespaces is not a substitute for scaling Workers.

heading: Scaling Workflows
subheading: How to reason about scaling — measure bottlenecks, not just open workflow count
description:
**Key distinction — do not choose Worker count based only on open workflows:**
• **Open workflows** — all executions not yet closed.
• **Ready tasks** — tasks that need a Worker right now.
• **Throughput** — how many tasks complete per second/minute.
• **Latency** — how long tasks wait and execute.

Many workflows may be waiting for timers, signals, or external events. 200,000 open workflows do NOT imply 200,000 Worker threads.

**Scaling approach:**
1. Measure workload and locate the bottleneck.
2. Monitor task queue backlog/age and schedule-to-start latency.
3. Scale Workflow Workers if Workflow Task processing/replay is the bottleneck.
4. Scale Activity Workers if Activity execution capacity is the bottleneck.
5. Tune pollers and concurrency limits.
6. Separate workload types using different task queues when isolation is useful.
7. Protect databases/APIs with rate limits, bounded concurrency, connection pools, and backpressure.
8. Check Temporal Server and persistence capacity separately.
9. Load-test representative workflow histories, activity duration, retries, and bursts.
10. Scale gradually and verify that throughput improves without increasing failures.

**What becomes the bottleneck?**
• High schedule-to-start latency → insufficient Worker/poller capacity or Temporal dispatch issues.
• High Activity execution latency → slow database/API or inefficient Activity code.
• High Worker CPU → CPU-heavy code, high replay cost, or too much work per Worker.
• Database connection exhaustion → too much Activity concurrency or undersized DB.
• Backlog continually increasing → arrival rate exceeds processing capacity.

**Worker Scaling vs Server Scaling:**
• **Worker scaling** — adds application execution capacity. Add replicas, CPU/memory, or tune concurrency/pollers. Helps when Workers cannot keep up.
• **Temporal Server scaling** — addresses server-side coordination, task dispatching, history operations, and persistence pressure.
• Adding Worker replicas does not fix a server/persistence bottleneck. Scaling the server does not add Activity execution capacity.

**Conceptual model:**
Effective throughput is limited by the minimum of Worker capacity, downstream capacity, and Temporal Server/persistence capacity.

heading: Monitoring & Metrics
subheading: What to monitor and what to alert on in a Temporal-powered system
description:
Monitor both Temporal and application dependencies.

**Useful signals:**
• Workflow Task schedule-to-start latency.
• Activity schedule-to-start latency.
• Activity execution latency.
• Activity failures and retries.
• Task queue backlog and backlog age.
• Workflow execution failures and latency.
• Worker CPU, memory, replica availability, and poller behavior.
• Database connection pool utilization and latency.
• External API latency and error rate.
• Temporal Server/persistence latency and resource pressure (when self-hosted).

**Alert on:**
• Sustained queue latency.
• Growing backlog age.
• Repeated Activity failures.
• Worker unavailability.
• Downstream saturation.

A large number of open workflows alone is not necessarily an incident.

heading: Temporal UI & Observability
subheading: Visibility into what your distributed workflows are doing
description:
Temporal provides a web UI that gives full visibility into every Workflow Execution. This solves one of the hardest problems in distributed systems — understanding what is happening across multiple services.

**What you can inspect:**
• Workflow ID and Run ID.
• Workflow type and input parameters.
• Current execution status (Running, Completed, Failed, Cancelled, Terminated, Timed Out).
• Pending Activities — which activities are currently running or waiting to be retried.
• Retry state — how many times an activity has been retried and why.
• Failure details — error messages and stack traces.
• Complete event history — every event in the workflow's lifecycle in order.
• Signal history — which signals were received and when.
• Timer status — when timers were set and when they fired.

This is invaluable for debugging distributed workflows. Instead of digging through logs from multiple services, you can trace the entire execution of a business process in one place.

**RPC (Remote Procedure Call):**
All communication between your application, Workers, and Temporal Server happens over RPC — specifically gRPC over HTTP/2. RPC allows one process to invoke an operation on another process as if it were a local function call. Your application sends StartWorkflowExecution RPC to start workflows. Workers use PollWorkflowTaskQueue and RespondWorkflowTaskCompleted RPCs to get and report work. This is the underlying communication mechanism that makes the distributed coordination work.

heading: Common Interview Questions
subheading: Quick-fire answers to the most frequently asked Temporal questions
description:
**Q:** Does Temporal Server execute my Workflow code?
**A:** No. Workflow and Activity code executes in your Worker processes. Temporal Server only coordinates and maintains durable state.

**Q:** Where does a Worker run?
**A:** In your infrastructure — inside your application process, Kubernetes pod, or a dedicated Worker service.

**Q:** What happens when a Worker crashes?
**A:** Temporal has the durable workflow history. Another Worker replays the history and continues the Workflow from where it left off.

**Q:** What is a Signal?
**A:** An asynchronous message sent to an existing Workflow Execution to provide it with new information.

**Q:** Does a Signal directly call a method on the Worker?
**A:** No. The signal goes to Temporal Server, is durably recorded, and is delivered to the Worker through the task/replay mechanism.

**Q:** Signal vs Activity?
**A:** A Signal provides information TO a workflow from the outside world. An Activity performs external work FROM a workflow.

**Q:** start() vs execute()?
**A:** start() is asynchronous — starts the workflow and returns immediately. execute() is synchronous — starts the workflow and blocks until it completes.

**Q:** Why must Workflow code be deterministic?
**A:** Because Temporal replays workflow history to reconstruct state. The code must make the same decisions during replay as it did during the original execution.

**Q:** What is a Task Queue?
**A:** A logical queue that routes Workflow Tasks or Activity Tasks to Workers polling that queue.

**Q:** What is durable execution?
**A:** The ability for a Workflow to continue reliably across process and machine failures because its state and history are durably managed by Temporal.

**Q:** What is RPC in Temporal's context?
**A:** Remote Procedure Call — the mechanism by which your application, Workers, and Temporal Server communicate over the network (using gRPC).

**Q:** What about business failures vs infrastructure failures?
**A:** Infrastructure failures (network timeout, service unavailable) can be retried automatically. Business failures (account not found, insufficient funds) require application-level logic — often the Saga/compensation pattern.

**Q:** What is sticky scheduling?
**A:** A performance optimization where Temporal prefers sending subsequent Workflow Tasks to the same Worker to reuse cached state. If that Worker is unavailable, another Worker replays history and continues — sticky scheduling is not a correctness guarantee.

**Q:** Does Temporal automatically version Workflow code?
**A:** No. Temporal provides versioning APIs (Workflow.getVersion / GetVersion), but the developer must identify incompatible changes and guard them. Arbitrary code changes are not automatically backward-compatible.

**Q:** Does Temporal have an Activity version API?
**A:** No general Activity-version API exists. Completed Activity results are in history and are not re-executed. Pending Activities run whatever implementation is on the Worker that picks them up. Use distinct activity types or Worker Versioning for controlled rollouts.

**Q:** How do you scale for 200,000 workflows?
**A:** Do not equate open workflows with required Workers. Measure ready tasks, throughput, and latency. Scale Workers and pollers based on actual bottlenecks — task queue backlog, schedule-to-start latency, and downstream capacity.

**Q:** What if more Workers do not improve throughput?
**A:** The bottleneck may be downstream (database, external API), Temporal Server/persistence, or misconfigured concurrency/pollers. Diagnose with metrics before adding more replicas.

**Q:** How do you deploy a Workflow change with 100,000 workflows running?
**A:** Use Workflow.getVersion to branch old vs new logic. Old histories replay the old path; new executions take the new path. Optionally use Worker Versioning to route executions to compatible Worker deployments.

heading: Final Mental Model
subheading: The core truths to internalize about Temporal
description:
**1.** Temporal Server coordinates and persists. Workers execute your code.

**2.** Durable execution means workflow progress survives infrastructure failures because history is persisted and replayed.

**3.** Determinism is required for replay correctness. All side effects go through Activities.

**4.** Scaling requires measurement — open workflows ≠ required Workers. Identify bottlenecks with metrics.

**5.** Workflow code changes require explicit compatibility handling (Workflow.getVersion or equivalent).

**6.** Activity code changes affect only future executions of that Activity. Completed results are in history.

**7.** Sticky scheduling is a performance optimization, not a correctness guarantee.

**8.** Task queues route work. Namespaces isolate administration. Neither is a substitute for scaling Workers.

**9.** Monitor schedule-to-start latency, backlog age, Activity failures, Worker health, and downstream capacity.

**10.** Temporal handles the infrastructure complexity of distributed coordination. You handle business logic and compatibility.
